messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Speaking of time-series examples...
parts:
Pertinent to the recent request for time-series examples, I came across this post (http://www.r-bloggers.com/additive-modelling-global-temperature-time-series-revisited/) that uses generalized additive modelling to look at global temperature data. Because I'm obsessed with Gaussian Process models of late, I thought I'd see how one would fare with this data set. 

Here's a gist with my attempt: https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/770aceab99bac256f89bcc62c35fa3d2

Here's the plot of the data with grey 95% credible interval on posterior samples (y2) and a green 95% credible interval on the mean function (mu2):



Now, I'm actually not sure whether it's the grey ribbon or green ribbon (or neither?) that would be the appropriate analog to the ribbon computed in the post above using GAM; the grey (y2) is far wider than the GAM ribbon while the green (mu2) is far narrower. Furthermore, if I try the computation of the first derivative as in the GAM post, for the y2 data I get what looks to be a uniform band:



while for mu2 I get something very much like that displayed in the GAM post, but with (again) far narrower bands:



Is something awry here, or is it really that with GPs we can get such higher certainty on the mean function?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Re: Speaking of time-series examples...
parts:
The results between the GP method and the GAM method look quite different on the right hand side tail of the first derivative plot,  The r-bloggers plot has the first derivative above 1% and your plot has the first derivative tending to 0%. Your graph suggests a slowdown in temperatures increasing, but not the r-bloggers post.

Very interesting!


Also, your choice of priors seems worth investigating.  Perhaps changing the priors to something non-informative might make a difference.  Perhaps you could try cauchy priors?

Finally, there could be a change point in the data.  Try splitting the data from 1950 onwards and see if the hyperparameters change.

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Speaking of time-series examples...
parts: On Mon, Apr 4, 2016 at 5:21 PM, WallSt <how...@zail.org> wrote:

The results between the GP method and the GAM method look quite different on the right hand side tail of the first derivative plot,  The r-bloggers plot has the first derivative above 1% and your plot has the first derivative tending to 0%. Your graph suggests a slowdown in temperatures increasing, but not the r-bloggers post.

I wonder if this difference might be more trivially attributed to the mean-reversion behaviour at the edges induced by my re-scaling of the data and use of a 0 mean vector. I'm guessing that GAM prefers to just stay in the region of the local data.
Also, your choice of priors seems worth investigating.  Perhaps changing the priors to something non-informative might make a difference.  Perhaps you could try cauchy priors?

I chose the priors to be fairly wide-yet-reasonably shaped defaults  (i.e. avoiding cauchy for poor sampling behaviour as noted in other threads here, and using a non-zero-mode for sigma & eta). Switching to cauchy(0,4) for all the hyperparameters (rho, sigma, eta) yields much slower sampling (lower ESS given constant time) but not particularly distinguishable posterior ribbons for the mean function.
Finally, there could be a change point in the data.  Try splitting the data from 1950 onwards and see if the hyperparameters change.
Neat idea!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speaking of time-series examples...
parts:
I mean the usual thing. I go over examples in a case
study on mc-stan.org and also cite Raftery et al.'s paper
on the topic:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/pool-binary-trials.html

The basic idea is that you want to make sure simulated parameter
values are within their posterior 50% intervals roughly 50% of
the time (nothing special about 50% --- you really want all the
intervals to be calibrated).

What you're talking about is posterior predictive checking, which
I also discuss in the above case study.

- Bob

Finally got around to playing with this again. I read up on calibration and see that indeed the model seems to be well-calibrated insofar as the 25%ile-75%ile band of the y2 samples indeed captures 50% of the data. 

However, when I run the model on just the even years, then again on just the odd years, there's substantial non-overlap of the resulting 95%ile bands of the samples for mu2 (mean function), supporting my previous observation that the bands for the mean function seem overly narrow. Presumably I'm incorrect in my interpretation of those bands as reflecting the credible range for the mean function of the data-generating process (since you wouldn't expect the credible range of this property to vary dramatically between odd & even years), so any idea what these bands are? More importantly, any idea what I'd need to do to compute what I thought those bands were (credible range for the mean function)?

Mike

Dalhousie University

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speaking of time-series examples...
parts:
Won't only using even or odd years in the time series affect
the scale of any kind of moving average function, so that you'd
be fitting different models?

You have to be careful with 95% intervals as they're very noisy
without a large effective sample size.

By captures 50% of the data, you mean the posterior predictive
50% intervals contain the true values around 50% of the time?

The real issue is that unless you have the true model, you
don't get guarantees on matching the true data generating process
with your estimates. This is the sense in which all stats, frequentist
and Bayesian, is subjective. For example, if I make a complete
pooling assumption for some item-specific effect, I'll get narrow
posterior intervals compared to assuming no pooling. But I am unlikely
to get good coverage if that complete pooling assumption is incorrect.

Another example is that if you assume normal noise and the noise
actually has fatter tails, then you can't get calibrated. Similarly
if you assume a Poisson or binomial distribution for counts or
repeated trials and the data's actually overdispersed.

- Bob

I've updated the gist to include the stan file for a new version of the model where, instead of trying to derive the mean function of a GP in the transformed parameters section, I explicitly model a noiseless latent GP that is then sampled with noise to create the data. The resulting posterior on the latent function seems much more reasonable as a predictive band:



However, this new model samples rather slowly :O\ At least, I think it does. The above plot certainly looks nice and smooth, but it's from a 4-chain run of iter=2e3 where each chain took about 10 minutes and the resulting ESS for the GP parameters are fairly low (eta=68, rho=39, noise=16).

Mike L, I just looked at your gp_fit_2.stan. My guess is that the low ESS/second may be a function of the centered parameterization that you're using for f. With a non-centered parameterization for f, I get something like 400 ESS on 1000 post-warmup samples from NUTS for rho, eta and noise. The reparameterized model is attached with some fatter (default) half-cauchy(0, 2.5) priors on rho, eta and noise.

Given that you're increasing the number of parameters from 3 to around 170, it's not especially surprising that the wall-time for running a single chain should increase.

Betancourt, I do get some posterior correlation between log(rho) and log(eta), but I'm not getting the banana plots that I'm used to for non-identifiable models.

Rob

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speaking of time-series examples...
parts:
I went quiet yesterday as I tried out the various suggestions and tweaks thereon:

Andrew suggested a more concentrated prior on the lengthscale. I had the GP coded as in the manual where rho=1/lengthscale, which I find more intuitive as the values from 0-1 imply near-monotonicity within the range of the data (if x is scaled to 0-1), making the typical peaked-at-zero priors sensibly reflecting a bias for simpler functions. 

That said, switching from rho~student_t(4,0,1) to rho~normal(0,1) indeed improved things quite a bit such that when I ran 4 chains at iter=2e3 they were about 5 mins each, had ESS for the noise & eta parameters in the thousands and rho >100. 

Curiously, the 2.5%ile-97.5%ile ribbon of the posterior samples on f (the noiseless latent GP) didn't differ considerably from the earlier example with low ESS on the parameters. I also tried Rob's non-centered version which takes more wall time but indeed has a higher ESS. However, the ribbon on f came out very different this time, seemingly far too smooth.
